content: Neglected diseases are a group of tropical infections that predominantly affect low-income populations in developing regions of Africa, Asia, and the Americas. These diseases are defined differently by various organizations, but collectively, they are responsible for an estimated 500,000 to 1 million deaths annually and contribute to a global disease burden comparable to that of HIV/AIDS. Unlike the big three diseases (HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria), which receive significant media attention and research funding, neglected diseases are often overlooked. Some of these diseases have known preventive measures or effective treatments available in developed countries, but these interventions are not universally accessible in poorer regions. In some cases, the treatments are relatively inexpensive, costing as little as $20 per child per year. Diseases Overview Trypanosomal Parasites Kala-azar (Visceral Leishmaniasis): This severe form of leishmaniasis has existing treatments, and vaccines were under development as of 2006. African Sleeping Sickness (African Trypanosomiasis): This disease was nearly eradicated in the 20th century, but a relaxation in control measures has led to its resurgence. While treatments exist, they are highly toxic, and resistance is spreading. If untreated, the disease is always fatal. It is transmitted through the bite of the tsetse fly. Chagas Disease (American Trypanosomiasis): There is no vaccine for Chagas disease. Treatments for early infection exist but are not cost-effective and are not officially authorized. Current drugs have severe side effects. Chagas disease does not kill rapidly but causes years of debilitating chronic symptoms. It is spread through bites from South American assassin bugs. Some historians speculate that Charles Darwin may have contracted Chagas disease during his voyage on the HMS Beagle. Worm (Helminth) Parasites Schistosomiasis: This disease can be treated with inexpensive praziquantel, but reinfection cannot be prevented. Other treatments are harder to access in developing countries. Multiple vaccines are under development. Schistosome species have a complex life cycle alternating between humans and freshwater snails, with infection occurring through contact with contaminated water. The damage is caused not by the worms themselves but by the large volume of eggs they produce. Lymphatic Filariasis (Elephantiasis): Anthelmintic treatments are under investigation. Onchocerciasis (River Blindness): Anthelmintic treatments exist, and prevention involves insect control. Dracunculiasis (Guinea Worm): Eradication was targeted for 2009, as of 2007. Soil-Transmitted Helminthiases: Ascariasis (Roundworm): Anthelmintic treatments exist, and prevention involves food and sewage sanitation. Trichuriasis (Whipworm): Anthelmintic treatments exist, and prevention involves food and sewage sanitation. Hookworm: Anthelmintic treatments exist, and prevention involves food and sewage sanitation. Bacterial Infections Leprosy: Antibiotic treatments are available. Buruli Ulcer: Surgical and antibiotic interventions are recommended. Trachoma: Antibiotic treatments exist, and prevention involves interpersonal hygiene. Cholera: Caused by Vibrio cholerae bacteria in contaminated drinking water, cholera presents with severe, watery diarrhea after an incubation period of 0–5 days. It can kill patients within 24 hours due to rapid dehydration. Antibacterial treatments can cure the disease, but isotonic fluid replacement therapy is the most effective, reducing mortality to 1% of cases. Cholera can be partially prevented with two oral vaccines, but access to clean drinking water is the most reliable preventive measure. Viral Infections Yellow Fever: A vaccine exists for yellow fever, which is caused by a flavivirus. Dengue Fever: Also caused by a flavivirus, dengue fever is spread by the Aedes aegypti mosquito. While not usually fatal, infection with one of four serotypes increases susceptibility to other serotypes, potentially leading to the dangerous dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF). No specific treatment exists beyond palliative care. Japanese Encephalitis: This disease, also caused by a flavivirus, is spread by Culex tritaeniorhynchus mosquitoes.
